items.stem: In the linear model y = Xβ + u, y is 50×1 and X is 50×5 (the first column of X is the intercept). If R² = 0.55, the adjusted R² is (to three decimals)
items.explanation: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k), where k counts every column of X, the intercept included. Here 1 − (1 − 0.55) × 49/45 = 0.510. Trap: using n − k − 1 counts the intercept twice and gives 0.499.

items.stem: For the model yₜ = α + βxₜ + uₜ with uₜ = ρuₜ₋₁ + εₜ, the OLS residuals eₜ satisfy Σeₜ² ≈ 5.28 and Σeₜeₜ₋₁ ≈ 1.32 for a large n. The estimated ρ and the Durbin–Watson statistic are, respectively,
items.explanation: Estimate ρ by regressing each residual on the previous one: ρ̂ = Σeₜeₜ₋₁/Σeₜ² = 1.32/5.28 = 0.25. For large n the Durbin–Watson statistic is d ≈ 2(1 − ρ̂) = 1.50. Trap: 2(1 + ρ̂) has the sign the wrong way round; positive autocorrelation pushes d below 2.

items.stem: Consider the two-equation model (i) y₁ = γ₁y₂ + β₁₁ x₁ + β₁₂ x₂ + ε₁ and (ii) y₂ = γ₂y₁ + β₂₂ x₂ + ε₂, where the y's are endogenous and the x's are exogenous (all coefficients shown are non-zero). Then
items.explanation: With G = 2 equations, an equation is identified when it excludes at least G − 1 = 1 exogenous variable that appears elsewhere in the system (order condition; with two equations and non-zero coefficients this also satisfies the rank condition). (i) excludes no exogenous variable and (ii) excludes x₁, so: (ii) is identified but (i) is not. Trap: including more exogenous variables in an equation makes it harder, not easier, to identify.

items.explanation: With G = 2 equations, an equation is identified when it excludes at least G − 1 = 1 exogenous variable that appears elsewhere in the system (order condition; with two equations and non-zero coefficients this also satisfies the rank condition).
